title: Mundi origo
titleEn: The Origin of the World — Metamorphoses I.5–88
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: This is the poem's cosmogony, told immediately after Ovid's opening promise to sing of bodies changed into new forms. It begins with Chaos — not empty space but a shapeless mass in which the elements lay jammed together and at war — and follows the separation of fire, air, earth and water, the rounding of the earth into a globe, the pouring out of the seas and the rivers, the five zones of sky and land, the posting of the four winds to their quarters, and the stars breaking out at last across the whole sky. It ends with the making of man, upright and looking at the stars, in the likeness of the gods. Ovid does not name the world's maker — 'a god and a better nature' (21), 'whoever of the gods that was' (32) — and sets two accounts of man's origin side by side without choosing between them, though the second brings in Prometheus, named only as 'the one sown from Iapetus'. The vocabulary is borrowed from Greek and Roman natural philosophy ('semina rerum', the seeds of things), so the lines read as physics as much as myth. The Latin is dactylic hexameter and the sentences run freely across the verse lines, so the unit you tap often begins or ends in mid-line.

sentences.t:
Ante mare et terras et quod tegit omnia caelum
unus erat toto naturae vultus in orbe,
quem dixere chaos:
sentences.l:
Before the sea and the lands and the sky that covers all things,
there was one face of nature in the whole round world,
which they called Chaos:
sentences.i: Before there was sea, or land, or the sky that covers everything, nature wore a single face throughout the whole world, and they called it Chaos:
sentences.n: 'quod tegit omnia caelum' — the relative clause is folded into the list, so the third item is 'the sky, which covers all things'. 'unus… vultus' (one face) is pulled apart around 'toto naturae', the noun and its adjective held at opposite ends of the line — normal in verse, and worth putting back together as you read. 'dixere' = 'dixerunt', the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ēre; it is everywhere in Ovid, so meet it once here and it will not trip you again. Greek 'chaos' is not disorder in the modern sense but a yawning, unformed gap, and Ovid spends the next lines defining it.

sentences.t:
rudis indigestaque moles
nec quicquam nisi pondus iners congestaque eodem
non bene iunctarum discordia semina rerum.
sentences.l:
a raw and unsorted mass,
and nothing but a lifeless weight, and heaped in the same place
the warring seeds of things not well joined.
sentences.i: a rough, unsorted mass — nothing but inert weight, and, piled up in the one spot, the quarrelling seeds of things that had never been properly joined.
sentences.n: 'indigesta' is 'not sorted out' (from 'digero', to arrange and distribute), not 'indigestible'. 'congesta' is neuter plural agreeing with 'semina', and 'eodem' is the adverb 'to the same place'. 'semina rerum' — the seeds of things — is the vocabulary of natural philosophy, the standing Latin term for the first particles of matter; Ovid is writing physics here as much as myth.

sentences.t:
nullus adhuc mundo praebebat lumina Titan,
nec nova crescendo reparabat cornua Phoebe,
sentences.l:
No Titan yet offered his light to the world,
nor did Phoebe by growing restore her new horns,
sentences.i: As yet no Titan gave the world his light, nor did Phoebe, waxing, make her horns new again,
sentences.n: Titan is the Sun and Phoebe the Moon — the heavenly bodies named by divine epithet, which Latin verse does constantly. 'cornua' are the horns of the crescent, and the moon 'repairs' them month by month; 'crescendo' is an ablative gerund, 'by waxing'. 'mundo' is dative with 'praebebat', 'offered to the world'.

sentences.t:
nec circumfuso pendebat in aere tellus
ponderibus librata suis, nec bracchia longo
margine terrarum porrexerat Amphitrite;
utque aer, tellus illic et pontus et aether.
sentences.l:
nor did the earth hang in the air poured round about it,
balanced by its own weights, nor along the long
rim of the lands had Amphitrite stretched out her arms;
and as air was, so earth was there, and sea, and aether.
sentences.i: nor did the earth hang balanced on its own weight in the air that flows about it; nor had Amphitrite reached her arms along the long edge of the lands; and where the air was, there too were earth and sea and the upper air.
sentences.n: Amphitrite, Neptune's consort, stands for the sea itself, and her 'arms' are the water reaching along the coastlines. 'ponderibus librata suis' — 'balanced by its own weights' — is the Greek physical idea that the earth stays put because it is in equilibrium with itself and needs nothing to hold it up. Line 15 is a hard spot: the edition prints 'utque aer… et aether' with no verb of its own, so a verb has to be carried over from what precedes — 'and as air was there, so were earth and sea and aether', all in one place at once. Other editions print 'utque erat et tellus illic et pontus et aer', which supplies 'erat'; either way the point is that the four had no separate places.

sentences.t:
Sic erat instabilis tellus, innabilis unda,
lucis egens aer:
sentences.l:
So the land was not to be stood on, the water not to be swum,
the air in want of light:
sentences.i: So there was no standing on the land, no swimming in the water, and the air had no light in it:
sentences.n: 'instabilis' and 'innabilis' are built the same way — 'in-' plus a verb plus '-bilis', 'not able to be stood on', 'not able to be swum'; 'innabilis' is rare, and Ovid pairs the two for the chime. 'egens' takes the genitive, so 'lucis egens' is 'in need of light'.

sentences.t:
nulli sua forma manebat,
obstabatque aliis aliud, quia corpore in uno
frigida pugnabant calidis, umentia siccis,
mollia cum duris, sine pondere habentia pondus.
sentences.l:
for nothing did its own form remain,
and one thing stood in the others' way, because in one body
cold things fought with hot, wet with dry,
soft with hard, things without weight with things that had weight.
sentences.i: Nothing kept its own shape; each got in the others' way, because within a single body cold fought hot, wet fought dry, soft fought hard, and the weightless fought what had weight.
sentences.n: 'nulli' is dative — 'for nothing did its own form remain'. 'obstabatque aliis aliud' is the 'alius… alius' idiom, 'one thing… the others', and 'obsto' governs the dative. 'pugnabant' takes a plain ablative for what is fought against ('calidis', 'siccis'), then Ovid varies it with a preposition, 'cum duris'. The first two pairs are the standard contraries of Greek physics — hot against cold, wet against dry — and he runs on with soft against hard, weightless against weighty.

sentences.t: Hanc deus et melior litem natura diremit.
sentences.l: This strife a god — and a better nature — broke apart.
sentences.i: It was a god, and a better nature, that put an end to this quarrel.
sentences.n: 'hanc… litem' is split wide open around 'deus et melior natura', so the demonstrative comes first and the noun it belongs to only at the end. 'lis' is a lawsuit or dispute and 'dirimo' is the word for breaking one up, so the elements' fight is settled the way a case in court is settled. And note who settles it: Ovid says only 'a god and a better nature', declining to name the maker here or at line 32.

sentences.t:
Nam caelo terras et terris abscidit undas,
et liquidum spisso secrevit ab aere caelum.
sentences.l:
For from the sky he cut off the lands, and from the lands the waters,
and he separated the clear heaven from the thick air.
sentences.n: 'caelo… terris' are ablatives of separation with 'abscidit' — 'from the sky, from the lands', no preposition needed. The chain steps down in order: sky, then land, then water; then the clear upper heaven is parted from the dense air below. 'liquidum' here means clear and transparent, not 'liquid'.

sentences.t:
Quae postquam evolvit caecoque exemit acervo,
dissociata locis concordi pace ligavit.
sentences.l:
And after he had unrolled them and drawn them out of the blind heap,
he bound them, sundered in their places, in harmonious peace.
sentences.n: 'Quae' opening the sentence is the connecting relative — 'and these things', not a question; Latin uses a relative where English begins a new sentence with 'and them'. 'caecus' means both 'blind' and 'unseen, lightless': a heap in which nothing could be made out. The paradox is deliberate — by pulling them apart ('dissociata locis') he binds them ('ligavit') into a peace.

sentences.t:
Ignea convexi vis et sine pondere caeli
emicuit summaque locum sibi fecit in arce:
proximus est aer illi levitate locoque:
sentences.i: The fiery energy of the arching, weightless heaven leapt up and took its place in the highest stronghold; next to it, in lightness as in position, comes the air;
sentences.n: The genitive 'convexi… caeli' is split around the whole phrase: read 'the fiery force of the vaulted sky, which has no weight' — though 'et sine pondere' can equally be taken with 'vis', 'the fiery force, and weightless, of the vaulted sky'; either way what has no weight is fire. 'arx' is a citadel, the stronghold on the height — here the outermost shell of the sky. Ovid now sorts the four elements by weight, lightest first, each settling at its own level; and watch the present 'est' among the perfects, marking an arrangement that holds still.

sentences.t:
densior his tellus, elementaque grandia traxit
et pressa est gravitate sua: circumfluus umor
ultima possedit solidumque coercuit orbem.
sentences.l:
denser than these is earth: it drew the coarse elements down with it
and was pressed by its own heaviness; the water that flows around
took the last places and hemmed in the solid globe.
sentences.n: 'densior his' — comparative with the ablative of comparison, 'denser than these', i.e. than fire and air. 'traxit' is active and 'pressa est' passive in the same breath: earth drags the coarse matter down and is itself pressed down. 'ultima' (neuter plural) is 'the outermost parts'; 'circumfluus' — flowing round — is a rare compound, and the ocean is imagined as a ring closing the land in.

sentences.t:
Sic ubi dispositam quisquis fuit ille deorum
congeriem secuit sectamque in membra redegit,
principio terram, ne non aequalis ab omni
parte foret, magni speciem glomeravit in orbis.
sentences.l:
So when — whoever of the gods that was — he had cut the heap,
now laid in order, and reduced the cut mass into its limbs,
first the earth, lest it not be equal on every
side, he rolled into the shape of a great globe.
sentences.i: So, once he — whichever of the gods it was — had divided the mass now laid in order, and reduced the pieces he had cut into their several parts, he first rolled the earth into the shape of a great sphere, so that it should be the same on every side.
sentences.n: 'quisquis fuit ille deorum' — 'whoever of the gods that was'. Ovid drops the maker's identity into a parenthesis and leaves it unresolved, exactly as with 'a god and a better nature' at line 21; he does it a third time at 78–81. The physics is stated precisely, the theology left open. 'ne non aequalis… foret' is a double negative that comes out positive — 'so that it should not be unequal', i.e. equal all round; 'foret' is simply 'esset'. 'membra' (limbs) treats the world as a body being jointed, and 'glomeravit' is the verb for rolling something into a ball.

sentences.t:
Tum freta diffudit rapidisque tumescere ventis
iussit et ambitae circumdare litora terrae.
sentences.l:
Then he poured out the seas and bade them swell with rushing winds
and surround the shores of the encircled land.
sentences.n: 'iussit' governs two infinitives, 'tumescere' and 'circumdare', with 'freta' (the seas) as their subject: the water is under orders. 'ambitae terrae' is proleptic — the land is called 'encircled' by the very act being described, so it becomes what the participle already calls it.

sentences.t:
Addidit et fontes et stagna inmensa lacusque
fluminaque obliquis cinxit declivia ripis,
sentences.l:
He added springs too, and measureless pools and lakes,
and girdled the down-running rivers with slanting banks,
sentences.n: 'et… et… -que… -que' piles the waters into a list; the enclitic '-que' ('and', tacked onto the end of a word) is verse's favourite connector. 'declivia' is 'running downhill' and 'obliquis ripis' 'with banks set aslant' — the banks are what keeps a river in its channel, which matters for what comes next. 'inmensa' is the edition's spelling of 'immensa'.

sentences.t:
quae, diversa locis, partim sorbentur ab ipsa,
in mare perveniunt partim campoque recepta
liberioris aquae pro ripis litora pulsant.
sentences.l:
which, differing in their places, are in part swallowed by the earth herself,
in part reach the sea, and, received into the field
of freer water, beat on shores instead of banks.
sentences.i: and these, each scattered through its own region, are partly drunk down by the earth herself, and partly come through to the sea, where, taken into the open field of freer water, they beat upon shores instead of banks.
sentences.n: 'ab ipsa' — 'by her very self', the earth, which drinks some rivers down and never gives them back. 'partim… partim' is 'some… others'. The sea is a 'campus', a plain, of 'freer water' — open ground after the channel — and the rivers trade 'ripae' (river-banks) for 'litora' (sea-shores); Ovid keeps the two words carefully distinct. Line 42 is missing altogether from some editions, which end the sentence at 'perveniunt partim'.

sentences.t:
Iussit et extendi campos, subsidere valles,
fronde tegi silvas, lapidosos surgere montes.
sentences.l:
He bade the plains too be stretched out, the valleys sink,
the woods be covered with leaf, the stony mountains rise.
sentences.i: He bade the plains stretch wide, the valleys settle low, the woods be clothed in leaves, and the stony mountains climb.
sentences.n: Four infinitives hang from one 'iussit' — 'extendi' and 'tegi' passive, 'subsidere' and 'surgere' active — each with its own subject in the accusative: the accusative-and-infinitive that regularly follows a verb of ordering. 'fronde' is a collective singular, 'with foliage'.

sentences.t:
Utque duae dextra caelum totidemque sinistra
parte secant zonae, quinta est ardentior illis,
sic onus inclusum numero distinxit eodem
cura dei, totidemque plagae tellure premuntur.
sentences.l:
And as two zones cut the sky on the right and as many on the
left side, and a fifth is hotter than they,
so with the same number the god's care marked off the enclosed mass,
and just as many tracts are pressed upon the earth.
sentences.i: And just as two zones cut across the sky on the right and two on the left, with a fifth hotter than these, so by the same reckoning the god's forethought marked off the enclosed mass, and just so many belts are stamped upon the earth.
sentences.n: The five zones of the sky are standard Greek astronomy — two on either side of a burning middle one — and Ovid maps them straight down onto the globe, which is why the earth has five belts of climate too. 'utque… sic' is 'and just as… so'. 'cura dei' is the subject of 'distinxit' but is held back to the start of its own line. 'onus inclusum' is the earth, the mass shut in by the water of the last unit; 'tellure premuntur' is 'are pressed into the earth', the sky's five belts printed onto the globe below.

sentences.t:
Quarum quae media est, non est habitabilis aestu:
nix tegit alta duas: totidem inter utrumque locavit
temperiemque dedit mixta cum frigore flamma.
sentences.i: Of these belts the middle one cannot be lived in, because of the heat; deep snow covers two; and between the burning middle and each frozen end he set as many again, giving them a temperate climate by mixing flame with cold.
sentences.n: 'aestu' is ablative of cause — uninhabitable 'because of the heat'. 'inter utrumque' is 'between each of the two', that is, one temperate belt between the burning middle and each frozen end, which makes five in all. 'mixta cum frigore flamma' is an ablative of means with 'dedit', and it works like a recipe: the temperate blend is made 'by flame mixed with cold'.

sentences.t:
Inminet his aer. Qui quanto est pondere terrae,
pondere aquae levior tanto est onerosior igni.
sentences.l:
Above these hangs the air. And by as much as it is lighter than the weight
of earth, than the weight of water, by so much is it heavier than fire.
sentences.i: Above these hangs the air; and by exactly as much as it is lighter than earth and water, by that much it weighs more than fire.
sentences.n: 'inminet' (the edition's spelling of 'imminet') takes the dative, 'hangs over them'. 'quanto… tanto' is the ablative of degree of difference — 'by how much… by that much' — so this is a stated proportion, not a loose comparison. 'pondere terrae, pondere aquae' are ablatives of comparison after 'levior'. Air takes third place in the ranking by weight: heavier than fire, lighter than water and earth.

sentences.t:
Illic et nebulas, illic consistere nubes
iussit et humanas motura tonitrua mentes
et cum fulminibus facientes fulgura ventos.
sentences.l:
There he bade the mists, and there the clouds, take their station,
and the thunder that was to shake human minds,
and the winds that make the lightning-flash along with the bolt.
sentences.n: 'illic… illic' is repeated for insistence, and one 'consistere' serves all four accusatives — mists, clouds, thunder, winds. 'motura' is a future participle, 'about to shake': the thunder is named by the effect it will have on human minds before it is named at all. Ovid keeps 'fulmen' (the bolt that strikes) apart from 'fulgur' (the flash that is seen), and gives the making of both to the winds.

sentences.t:
His quoque non passim mundi fabricator habendum
aera permisit:
sentences.l:
To these too the world's builder did not grant the air
to be held everywhere:
sentences.i: Even to these the world's maker did not grant possession of the air at large:
sentences.n: 'his' is the winds, carried over from the line before. 'habendum… aera permisit' is a gerundive after 'permitto': he handed the air over 'to be held' by them — but 'non passim', not anywhere they please. 'fabricator' is a workman's word, the maker as craftsman, and it pairs with 'opifex' at line 79. Here 'quoque' really is the adverb 'too'; elsewhere the same letters can be 'quō-que', 'and by which', so it is always worth a second look.

sentences.t:
vix nunc obsistitur illis,
cum sua quisque regant diverso flamina tractu,
quin lanient mundum: tanta est discordia fratrum.
sentences.l:
even now they are scarcely held back,
though each governs his own blasts in a separate quarter,
from tearing the world to pieces: so great is the brothers' discord.
sentences.i: even now they are barely kept from tearing the world apart, though each governs his own gusts in his own separate quarter: so great is the quarrelling among these brothers.
sentences.n: 'obsistitur illis' is an impersonal passive with the dative — literally 'it is resisted to them', which is the only way an intransitive verb can be made passive; English has to turn it round into 'they are scarcely held back'. 'quin lanient' is the regular construction after a phrase of hindering: 'from tearing'. The winds are brothers, sons of Astraeus and the Dawn, and 'discordia' picks up 'discordia semina rerum' from line 9 — the old quarrel of the elements survives in them.

sentences.t:
Eurus ad Auroram Nabataeaque regna recessit
Persidaque et radiis iuga subdita matutinis;
sentences.l:
Eurus withdrew toward the Dawn and the Nabataean kingdoms
and Persia, and the ridges laid beneath the morning rays;
sentences.n: The four winds are now posted to the four quarters, and Ovid names each quarter by its country rather than by a compass point. Eurus is the east wind: 'ad Auroram' is 'toward the Dawn', the goddess's name doing the work of 'eastward'. The Nabataeans were an Arabian people, Petra their city; 'Persis' is Persia. 'iuga subdita radiis matutinis' are the mountain ridges 'placed under' the first light of morning.

sentences.t:
vesper et occiduo quae litora sole tepescunt,
proxima sunt Zephyro:
sentences.l:
Evening, and the shores that grow warm with the setting sun,
are nearest to Zephyrus;
sentences.n: Zephyrus is the west wind, so his quarter is named by sunset: 'vesper' is both evening and the west, and 'occiduo sole' is the going-down sun. 'tepescunt' is an inchoative verb (the '-sco' formation) — 'grow warm', not 'are warm'; 'madescit' two lines on has the same shape.

sentences.t:
Scythiam septemque triones
horrifer invasit Boreas:
sentences.l:
Scythia and the seven plough-oxen —
these shudder-bringing Boreas fell upon;
sentences.i: On Scythia and the seven stars of the Wain fell Boreas, the bringer of the shudder of cold;
sentences.n: 'septem triones' are the seven plough-oxen — the stars of the Great Bear, which wheel round the pole and never set — and written together as 'septemtriones' the phrase is simply the Latin word for the north. Scythia is the far north beyond the Black Sea. 'horrifer' ('bringing the shudder') is a compound made for this wind, and 'invasit' is a word of violence: Boreas did not settle in his quarter, he fell upon it.

sentences.t:
contraria tellus
nubibus adsiduis pluviaque madescit ab Austro.
sentences.l:
the land opposite
grows wet with unceasing clouds and rain from Auster.
sentences.n: 'contraria tellus' is the country facing Boreas' own — the south. Auster is the south wind, wet where Boreas is dry, so the two are opposed by climate as well as by position. 'madescit' is another inchoative, 'becomes wet'. 'adsiduis' is the edition's spelling of 'assiduis', 'unremitting'.

sentences.t:
Haec super inposuit liquidum et gravitate carentem
aethera nec quicquam terrenae faecis habentem.
sentences.l:
Above these he set the aether, clear and lacking weight
and having nothing of earthly dregs.
sentences.n: 'haec super' puts the preposition after its noun (anastrophe) — read 'super haec', 'above these things'; verse does this freely. 'careo' takes the ablative, so 'gravitate carentem' is 'lacking weight'. 'faex' is the sediment left in the bottom of a wine-jar: the aether is topmost precisely because none of that heavy residue is in it. 'aethera' keeps its Greek accusative ending.

sentences.t:
Vix ita limitibus dissaepserat omnia certis,
cum, quae pressa diu massa latuere sub illa,
sidera coeperunt toto effervescere caelo.
sentences.l:
Scarcely had he fenced all things off in this way with fixed boundaries,
when the stars, which long lay hidden pressed beneath that mass,
began to seethe out over the whole sky.
sentences.n: 'vix… cum' is the standard pairing for one thing following hard on another — 'scarcely had he… when' — and the surprise always sits in the 'cum' clause. 'latuere' is 'latuerunt', the -ēre perfect again (you had 'dixere' at line 7). 'effervescere' is a boiling word: the stars do not merely appear, they seethe up out of the dark. The edition prints 'quae pressa diu massa latuere sub illa', hidden beneath the mass; some editions print 'quae pressa diu fuerant caligine caeca', pressed down by blind darkness.

sentences.t:
Neu regio foret ulla suis animalibus orba,
astra tenent caeleste solum formaeque deorum,
cesserunt nitidis habitandae piscibus undae,
terra feras cepit, volucres agitabilis aer.
sentences.i: And so that no region should be left without living creatures of its own, the stars and the forms of the gods hold the floor of heaven; the waters gave way to the gleaming fish for their dwelling; the earth took the wild beasts, and the restless air the birds.
sentences.n: 'neu' is 'et ne', 'and so that… not'; 'foret' is 'esset', and 'orba' takes the ablative, 'bereft of'. Four habitats and their tenants in four lines, one verb apiece — and 'tenent' is present among the perfects, so the stars are holding heaven still. 'habitandae' is a gerundive agreeing with 'undae': the waters yielded 'to be dwelt in' by the fish. 'agitabilis' — easily set moving — is a rare word, matching the air's restlessness to the birds'.

sentences.t:
Sanctius his animal mentisque capacius altae
deerat adhuc et quod dominari in cetera posset.
sentences.l:
A living thing more holy than these, and more capable of a lofty mind,
was still lacking — one that could rule over the rest.
sentences.n: 'sanctius' and 'capacius' are neuter comparatives agreeing with 'animal', with 'his' as ablative of comparison, 'than these' — than the beasts, fish and birds just placed. 'capax' takes the genitive, so 'mentis capacius altae' is 'more able to hold a lofty mind'. 'quod… posset' is a relative clause of characteristic, with the subjunctive: 'of the sort that could rule the rest'.

sentences.t:
Natus homo est, sive hunc divino semine fecit
ille opifex rerum, mundi melioris origo,
sive recens tellus seductaque nuper ab alto
aethere cognati retinebat semina caeli;
sentences.l:
Man was born — whether that craftsman of things, the origin
of a better world, made him from divine seed,
or whether the earth, new and lately drawn off from the high
aether, still kept the seeds of the sky she was kin to;
sentences.i: Man was born: either that maker of things, the beginning of a better world, fashioned him out of divine seed, or else the earth, still new and only lately parted from the high upper air, kept in her the seeds of the sky she was born of;
sentences.n: 'sive… sive' sets two accounts of man's origin side by side and declines to choose — the third time in this part that Ovid leaves the maker open ('a god and a better nature', 21; 'whoever of the gods that was', 32). 'opifex' is a craftsman at his bench, and 'mundi melioris origo' stands in apposition to him. Both accounts turn on 'semen', seed: divine seed in the one, the sky's own seeds still lying in fresh soil in the other. 'cognati caeli' — the earth is the sky's blood-relation, having been cut from it only a moment ago in this very poem.

sentences.t:
quam satus Iapeto mixtam pluvialibus undis
finxit in effigiem moderantum cuncta deorum.
sentences.l:
and this earth, mixed with rainwater, the one sown from Iapetus
shaped into the likeness of the gods who govern all things.
sentences.i: and this earth the son of Iapetus mixed with rainwater and moulded into the likeness of the gods who govern all things.
sentences.n: 'quam' is a connecting relative reaching back to 'tellus' in the line before — 'and this earth'. 'satus Iapeto' is 'sown from Iapetus', that is Prometheus, whom Ovid names only by his father; 'Iapeto' is an ablative of origin. 'moderantum' is a shortened genitive plural of 'moderantium', 'of those governing'. Man is made of mud — earth worked up with rain — and yet in the image of the gods, and both halves of that sit in the one sentence.

sentences.t:
Pronaque cum spectent animalia cetera terram,
os homini sublime dedit, caelumque videre
iussit et erectos ad sidera tollere vultus.
sentences.l:
And while the other living creatures look face-down upon the earth —
he gave man a face lifted high, and bade him look upon the sky
and raise his countenance upright to the stars.
sentences.i: And whereas the other creatures look downward at the ground, to man he gave a face turned upward, and told him to look at the sky and lift his gaze straight to the stars.
sentences.n: 'prona' is a predicate adjective with 'animalia' — the beasts look at the earth in that tilted-forward posture, and the word carries the posture, not merely the direction. 'cum spectent' is concessive with the subjunctive, 'although they look'. 'homini' is dative, 'to man'. The sentence is built as a contrast of two postures and lands on its last words, 'ad sidera… vultus', the face turned to the stars. It is among the most quoted sentences in the poem.

sentences.t:
Sic, modo quae fuerat rudis et sine imagine, tellus
induit ignotas hominum conversa figuras.
sentences.l:
So the earth, which just now had been raw and without image,
was changed and put on the unknown shapes of men.
sentences.i: So the earth, which a moment before had been raw and shapeless, was transformed and put on the unfamiliar shapes of men.
sentences.n: 'rudis' picks up the very word used of the original mass at line 7, so the making of the world ends where it began, with 'raw' — and the first change in a poem of changes is complete. 'induit' is the verb for putting on clothing: the earth dresses herself in human forms. 'conversa' — 'turned about, changed' — answers the poem's opening promise of 'mutatas… formas', shapes changed; and 'ignotas' means these shapes had never been seen before, there being as yet nothing to know them by.
